newsitem.title: USA: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Stock vols steady, bond-driven.
newsitem.headline: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Stock vols steady, bond-driven.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. stock index options were little changed in calm trade dominated by bond market direction, as fear of a big pullback subsided after Friday's dramatic turnaround rally, traders said.
Focus appeared to have shifted to Friday's May U.S. employment report from last Friday's early selloff triggered by Intel Corp's bearish earnings projection.
"I think the sights are set on the employment figures coming out at the end of the week," said Jesse Stamer of TradeNet, a designated primary market maker at the Chicago Board Options Exchange.
"Basically, we'll react to the bond market," he added. "We were higher when bonds were higher this morning, and then we turned lower as bonds started going lower."

Volume in CBOE's S&P 100 index .OEX options was light, with the index up 0.80 point at 827.50 at 1130 CDT/1630 GMT. The OEX had opened firmer, dipped to negative territory and bounced back again in a relatively narrow range.

The CBOE volatility index .VIX, which reflects implied volatilities for near-month OEX options, was up 0.04 point at 22.16, at about the middle of a 20-25 range the index has been in for most of this year.
Traders said the market's outlook was mildly positive after Friday's reversal that followed an early plunge on Intel's warnings about its second quarter earnings projection.
"Intel has been a market leader, so you'd have expected the market to turn more bearish," a brokerage trader said.
"Friday was a very powerful reversal day, and usually that is bullish," agreed Jay Shartsis, director of options trading at R.F. Lafferty & Co.
"The only problem is that put/call ratio and the sentiment situation have deteriorated lately," he added. "I don't know if they're going to go up too much from here.
Shartsis noted that recent rises in implied volatilities for out-of-the-money OEX calls relative to those for equally low-delta puts were alarming.

"Puts have come down and the calls have expanded to a point where...in the past you didn't have much upside," he said, referring to the contrarian nature of the market's put/call preference. "The expansion in call implied volatilities is not particularly bullish."
Both volume and implied volatility levels for puts had ballooned in early April, when the market's latest rally started.
